name: AppLess (Thesys)
what: Experimental demo of a phone with no apps - every screen generated by an LLM on demand, streamed, and rendered as real native components (Cupertino/Material 3) via the OpenUI spec. Expo SDK 54 / React Native, Cerebras for generation.
priceDetail: Free / MIT. Needs a Cerebras API key. The commercial upstream (Thesys OpenUI Cloud / C1 API) is priced separately.
notes: Generative UI - an LLM emitting a constrained component contract that renders in your own design system rather than free-form HTML - is the pattern most likely to matter for your design-system and Foundry work.
Reproducing the demo is the wrong thing to build. The reusable asset is the schema-constrained render contract, worth prototyping against Foundry's design tokens. The phone-OS framing is a tech demo.

Read as a pattern study, not a dependency. 4 commits and no releases means no maintenance story, and the integrations are simulated. Needs a Cerebras API key. The serious upstream is thesysdev/openui plus Thesys's commercial OpenUI Cloud / C1 API - price that separately before building a client feature on it.
adminNote: Read as a pattern study. The reusable asset is the schema-constrained render contract, not the phone-OS demo.

name: GatherOS
what: Local-first macOS app for capturing, organising and searching design references - drag, paste and screenshot capture, X bookmark sync, AI visual search, colour search, auto-tagging, unlimited libraries, and Figma-like open-canvas 'Spaces' for moodboarding. Companion Chrome extension saves from X, Instagram, Cosmos and any page.
priceDetail: Free while in public beta. Paid pricing not announced - assume a paid tier lands when beta ends.
notes: Solid for the studio's reference and moodboard workflow feeding concept and design-system work, but single-machine and Mac-only so it will not serve as a shared team library.
A native Mac app with local storage, browser extension, social sync and AI visual and colour search is months of work in a stack you probably do not want to own.

'Free' is a beta state, not a commitment - paid pricing has not been announced, so do not build a team process on it yet. Real limitations: macOS only, no web or mobile, no cloud sync (library lives on one machine, so no team sharing and backup is your problem), no semantic search, no agent or MCP integration. Small user base but actively maintained and pre-1.0.

name: meat (Bold Software)
what: Go CLI that uses a model to abridge a code diff into a 'reading diff' - stripping style and nil-check noise so a reviewer sees only conceptual and architectural changes. Explicitly aimed at humans reviewing agent-generated code.
priceDetail: Free / Apache 2.0. Real cost is model tokens on large diffs - verify before putting in CI.
notes: If you ship AI-written code for clients, this attacks the main quality bottleneck in that workflow - reviewing large agent diffs.
The mechanism is a chunked diff-splitter plus a well-tuned prompt - reproducible in a day. The only real asset is prompt quality, so use theirs rather than reinvent it.

14 stars means a credible experiment from a strong team (same org as sketch.dev), not a maintained product. README warns processing a commit takes a while and multi-MB diffs are chunked, so cost and latency scale with diff size. Which model/API key it needs is not documented - verify token spend before putting it in CI.
adminNote: Try the Apache-2.0 tool before writing our own. Verify model cost on large diffs.

name: oil-motion
what: NOT a JavaScript motion library despite the name. It is an agent Skill for Claude Code that designs an interactive animation, generates keyframe images, calls an AI video model for the in-between motion, compresses the result into web assets (WebP sprite sheets, MP4, frame sequences) and maps playback 0-100% to scroll, pointer, drag, touch, orientation or audio.
priceDetail: Free / MIT to use. Real cost is per-render AI video credits via ZenMux (MiniMax) - budget this per project.
notes: A genuinely new capability - art-directed, semantic motion for scroll-driven hero sections that you currently cannot produce without a motion designer.
MIT and installable as a skill in an afternoon. Rebuilding means a video-gen pipeline plus ffmpeg frame processing plus a scroll-mapped runtime, for no commercial upside.

Do not let this get mis-sold internally as a Motion/GSAP replacement. Those animate live DOM properties with tiny payloads; oil-motion animates pre-rendered pixels, so the deliverable is video or sprite sheets - heavy, not responsive, not screen-reader accessible, not text-selectable, cannot adapt to dynamic content or theming. No bundle-size claim anywhere, which is telling. Single maintainer, days-old code, primary SKILL.md is in Chinese, hard dependency on a paid third-party API, and needs Python 3, Pillow, ffmpeg and ffprobe locally. Specialist asset generator for one-off hero moments only - budget the render spend into the quote. Star count came from Trendshift and SkillsMP, not the repo header, which rendered inconsistently.

name: Originkit
what: Free animated component library ('largest free animated component library'), React and Framer variants, copy directly or pull via MCP. The link filters to the text-animation category.
priceDetail: Free. No paid tier, but also no licence published - treat that as a blocker for client work.
notes: Useful as a free grab-bag of text and animation effects for marketing-site builds, but too shallow and unproven to base a repeatable component pipeline on.
Individual text-animation effects are a few hours each with Motion or CSS. Take inspiration and the odd effect, not a dependency.

Thinnest item in the batch. No licence, attribution terms, component count or team disclosed anywhere on the site - no licence means no clear right to ship these in client work, so treat that as a blocker until confirmed. Framer-first positioning suggests the React exports are secondary. Effects skew showy rather than production-useful. Transitions.dev is the serious option.

name: ui.camera
what: Free browser tool that turns flat UI screenshots into 'product photography for software' - upload an image, manipulate 3D rotation on X/Y/Z, aspect ratio, aperture and depth of field, autofocus and zoom, then capture and export PNG.
priceDetail: Free. No pricing, tiers or sign-in anywhere on the site; monetisation model undisclosed.
notes: Useful for dressing up client app screenshots in case studies, proposals and your own portfolio without a designer mocking things up in Figma or Blender.

A WebGL plane with a texture, perspective camera controls, a shader depth-of-field pass and canvas export. A competent front-end dev could ship a rough version in a weekend - but it is free, so there is no reason to.

No about page, footer, credits, company name or social handle anywhere - the maker is genuinely unidentified, so provenance and longevity are unknown. Maximum-quality export requires their Chrome extension downloaded as a raw ZIP rather than from the Chrome Web Store, which means manual unpacked install, no store review and no auto-updates. Given it will need page-capture permissions, think twice before installing it on a machine holding client work. The in-browser version needs no install and is the safer default.

name: Flaude
what: Figma-side tool that copies real app screens and multi-step flows into Figma as editable layers rather than flat screenshots, then lets you redesign them via a Claude MCP connection. The /browse page is the free library of hundreds of web and iOS screens from Uber, Airbnb, Spotify, Netflix and similar.
priceDetail: Free (browse all, copy samples only); Pro $12.58/mo billed yearly = $151/yr; Team $450/yr for 3 seats; a Lifetime option exists but no figure published. Self-hosting offered as an alternative.
notes: Fast route from 'what do the best apps do for checkout and onboarding' to editable Figma layers you can restyle into a client's design system - it compresses the reference-gathering and first-draft stage.
The library is a continuous capture operation, not a feature. At ~$151/yr it is far cheaper than staffing the pipeline; the plugin and MCP plumbing is the easy part.

Two cautions. IP: you are copying other companies' UI and trade dress into Figma - fine as internal reference, dangerous if any survives into a client deliverable, so set a house rule that Flaude output gets fully restyled. Vendor risk: solo/indie with no company details, and Pro depends on a hosted MCP; the open-source repo mitigates this only if it actually has a licence, which I could not confirm. Check the plugin's terms before installing on a client-shared Figma org.
adminNote: House rule: Flaude output gets fully restyled before it goes anywhere near a client deliverable.

name: Refero Styles
what: Curated library of 2,000+ machine-readable design systems extracted from real product websites. Each entry exposes colours, type, spacing, components and a DESIGN.md you can drop into Cursor, Claude Code or v0.
priceDetail: Free to browse. Pro subscription required for the MCP/automation path (8,000 tool calls/mo). No price published - get it in writing.
notes: You already store design tokens in Foundry, so machine-readable token sets are a direct input to both design-system work and AI-assisted build.
Scraping computed styles into a DESIGN.md is a couple of days. Curating 2,000 systems is the bit you cannot copy - use theirs, build your own extractor only for client sites.

These are other companies' design systems reverse-engineered from live sites. Fine as reference and benchmarking, dubious as a shortcut for producing a client's brand. Beta, so spot-check spacing/component accuracy. Pricing is opaque - confirm before wiring a workflow to it.
adminNote: Free browsing is a benchmarking reference. Get the Pro price in writing before wiring MCP into a workflow.

name: Transitions.dev
what: Copy-paste library of 36+ production-ready UI transitions (card resize, modal, button, text effects) in CSS and React, plus an agent skill that installs them into a project and a live tuning tool. By Jakub Antalik.
priceDetail: Free tier. Pro $9/mo solo or $149 one-time lifetime. Team $39/mo for 5 seats or $499 lifetime. Commercial licence, unlimited projects.
notes: Motion is the fiddliest, most time-expensive polish layer on client builds. $149 lifetime pays back on one project's animation work.
You could write 36 transitions, but the value is the taste and the tuned easing curves. Recreating that judgement costs far more than $149.

Best value item in the batch. Single maintainer, so lifetime tier carries bus-factor risk - though you own the copied code, so abandonment costs future additions, not working projects. Verify the commercial licence covers redistribution inside client deliverables, not just your own products. Check the free companion repo first.
adminNote: Best value item in the batch. Buy the $149 lifetime, but confirm the commercial licence covers client deliverables first.

name: Wonder (Aquila Labs)
what: AI design tool where you generate and edit UI on a canvas that maps 1:1 to code, exporting production-ready React + Tailwind with no handoff. Exposes an MCP endpoint for coding agents.
priceDetail: Free $0 (3 private files, limited tokens). Pro $16/user/mo billed yearly, includes $20/mo AI tokens. Enterprise custom. Also on X as @usewonder.
notes: Design-and-build plus design systems is your core business, and this targets exactly the Figma-to-code handoff bottleneck.
An equivalent means a canvas engine, layout-to-JSX compiler, AI generation, realtime collaboration and a shader library. Multi-year product company, not an agency side project.

Public Alpha is their own label - expect breaking changes, do not put a client deadline on it. Pro's $20 token allowance is a cap, not unlimited. Figma is not mentioned anywhere, so assume no Figma round-trip, which is a real gap if client work starts in Figma. Unlikely to replace Foundry's token layer.
adminNote: Internal projects only while it is in public alpha — no Figma round-trip, so not for a client deadline.

name: Appllama
what: Design research platform cataloguing the screens of top-grossing iOS apps - around 770 apps and 30,900+ screens, added weekly - so you can study onboarding, paywalls and flows from apps that demonstrably make money, alongside their revenue, download and ratings data. Sold to designers and, explicitly, to AI agents via MCP credits.
priceDetail: Free (welcome screens, 2 newest apps rotating). Pro $12/mo billed yearly ($144/yr) or $20/mo monthly. Team $16/seat/mo annual ($192/yr per seat), 2-seat minimum. Enterprise custom. Pro and Team include 1,500 MCP credits/month.
notes: Strong for the pitch and discovery phase of native app work - 'here is how the top-grossing apps in your category handle paywalls' is a credible proposal input - but it is iOS-only, so it does little for the web builds that are most of your work.
Recreating it means continuously capturing and tagging ~31k screens across 760+ apps and joining them to paid App Store intelligence data - a permanent operations cost that dwarfs $144/yr.

Direct overlap with Flaude: Flaude gives editable Figma layers, Appllama gives screens plus commercial performance data. Paying for both is only justified if you do real native iOS work. The MCP angle is the interesting bit - Foundry or Claude Code could query it during a project - but the 1,500-credit ceiling has no published per-call cost, so budgeting is guesswork until you test it. Same IP caution as Flaude: reference, never a deliverable. Site claims design teams at ChatGPT, Strava and Duolingo as users - unverified social proof. Internal inconsistency between 770 apps (pricing page) and 762+ (homepage), so do not quote a precise number to clients.

name: Doppio (via Toolfolio listing)
what: Browser tool that turns static designs, images or Figma links into animated motion reels from code-based templates. The link itself is just a directory entry for it.
priceDetail: Free (2 projects, 5 credits, 4K export). Starter $29/mo billed quarterly. Power $58/mo quarterly. Power for Life $409 one-time. PAYG $29 per 10 credits.
notes: Solves a real agency chore - turning finished client UI into a polished showreel for case studies and pitches without opening After Effects.
An equivalent needs a browser compositor, template system, headless render farm and 4K encoding. Months of work for pure marketing output, not billable delivery.

No company or founder named on the site. The '5 of 100 remaining' lifetime counter and quarterly-only billing are pre-revenue indie signals - treat continuity risk as real and do not make it a dependency in a client-facing workflow. Credit model gets expensive on a heavy showreel month.

name: Hejour
what: Day-based notes app for Mac and iPhone where every day is a page, days link to each other with @ mentions, and todos carry reminders. Notes stored locally as plain Markdown, synced optionally via your own iCloud - no Hejour servers or accounts. Built solo by Enes Genç.
priceDetail: Free tier with no trial clock (unlimited daily notes, todos, search, iPhone sync, imports; capped at 3 linked days and 2 snippets). Pro $19 pay once, covering Mac and iPhone - unlimited linked days, calendar integration, sync across 3 Macs, images, code blocks, Vim mode, lifetime updates.
notes: Genuinely useful as a personal daily work log - what got done on which client, day by day - but single-user and local-first, so it will never be a shared team system alongside Foundry.
$19 once for a polished, notarised, local-Markdown Mac and iOS app is below the cost of a weekend of your own time, and Foundry already owns the multi-user side of this problem.

Local-first Markdown plus your own iCloud is the real selling point - no lock-in, files stay readable if the app dies. Downside is exactly that: personal tool, no shared workspace, one-person indie project, so treat 'lifetime updates' with the usual scepticism. Distributed via GitHub releases rather than the Mac App Store, which matters if you have device-management policies.

name: LogoCreator (logo-creator.io)
what: Free open-source AI logo generator - enter a company name, pick type, style and colours, get logo variations. Aimed at small businesses and founders.
priceDetail: 2 free credits on sign-in, no paid tier figures published. Self-hostable free with your own Together AI key (billed per image).
notes: Raster AI logo output is not usable as a client brand deliverable. At best a throwaway mood-board or placeholder generator.
It is a thin Next.js wrapper around Flux Pro on Together AI plus Clerk and Upstash. Fork it if you want a branded version, but there is no product here.

Genuinely a wrapper with no moat - value sits entirely in the Flux model and prompt presets. Two agency gotchas: output is bitmap not vector, so no clean SVG for a design system; and generated marks carry trademark and originality risk you should not pass to a paying client. Confirm licence terms before forking commercially.

name: Maccess (with 'Mackie' AI)
what: Despite the name it has nothing to do with accessibility. It is an iPhone app plus a required Mac helper for remote-controlling your Mac - virtual touchpad, keyboard, screen mirroring, file transfer, lock/sleep/restart, and an AI assistant called Mackie that runs automated tasks on the Mac. By Appic Marketing LLC. Needs iOS 17+ and macOS 14+.
priceDetail: Free tier (core touchpad and keyboard control, 1 paired Mac) and a Pro tier (screen mirroring, Mackie AI, unlimited Macs). No price figures published anywhere - you must install the app to see them. Some advanced AI modes need your own Claude Code or provider account.
notes: A personal remote-control convenience tool, not an audit, delivery or client-facing tool. The only agency angle is remotely poking a build machine or a Mac mini running a long task.

A real equivalent means a signed and notarised macOS helper daemon, low-latency screen streaming, Accessibility and Screen Recording entitlements, secure pairing and an iOS client. Expensive and off-mission.

IMPORTANT: the name reads like an accessibility product (Mac + access). It is not. It will not help run WCAG audits on client sites - no contrast checks, no axe or ARIA tooling, nothing. If it landed on an accessibility list it was mis-filed. Second flag: no public pricing at all, and the Mackie assistant executing tasks on your Mac has obvious security implications on a machine holding client code.

name: Path.cv
what: Hosted personal-site builder - upload a PDF CV and it converts to a live site, or build from templates. Includes a browsable public directory of users filterable by skill, location and profession.
priceDetail: Free on a path.cv subdomain. Pro $10/mo, or $6/mo billed annually.
notes: Serves individuals building their own CV site - closer to a downmarket substitute for what you sell than a tool you would use.

A CV-to-templated-site generator is genuinely small for a team with a design system and deploy pipeline, but at $10/mo against Framer, Bento, Super and LinkedIn it is a commodity market with no room for an agency to earn from it.

Two things worth weighing: it is a mild commodity-pressure signal at the very bottom of the market, relevant only if you ever quote cheap one-page personal sites; and the two-sided directory is the only interesting mechanic, but directories are hard to keep alive. Operator undisclosed - treat continuity as uncertain before recommending to a client.

name: TinyFolder
what: Native macOS app that groups applications into custom folders pinned to the Dock so you can open apps from a themed folder with one click. Made solo by Sergey Filkov. Requires macOS 13+.
priceDetail: Starter free - 1 folder, up to 4 apps. Lifetime Pro for 2 Macs $32 once - unlimited folders and apps, full Design Studio, 64 presets, 4 icon packs, global shortcuts, all future updates. 14-day money-back guarantee.
notes: Desktop cosmetics and launcher ergonomics for one machine. Touches nothing in client delivery, design systems or production readiness.
Reimplementing Dock-integrated folders, icon rendering and a preset and theming studio in AppKit is weeks of fiddly native work for a utility costing $32 once.

Worth flagging as a design-craft reference more than a tool: a tightly-scoped indie Mac product with a clean free-to-lifetime upgrade ladder, and a marketing site worth stealing patterns from for productised agency offers. Pro licence covers 2 Macs, so a team needs multiple purchases.

name: Halo (meethalo.app)
what: iPhone-only private AI assistant pulling mail, calendar, reminders, health and music into one daily briefing, triggering actions in third-party apps over MCP, with all processing claimed on-device. Consumer product, not team or agency.
priceDetail: Halo Lifetime $49 early bird, stated regular price $99, one-time, 7-day trial. No subscription tier. Product is not shipping yet.
notes: Single-user consumer iPhone assistant with no client, project or team dimension. Does nothing for agency delivery or Foundry.
Not worth building or copying - an on-device iOS assistant with EventKit/HealthKit/Mail permissions plus an MCP client is a months-long native project, and none of it serves agency ops.

Be sceptical: a pre-launch landing page selling a lifetime licence for a product that is not shipping. $49 upfront for a promise, no App Store listing to check reviews against, no company track record on the page. 'All on-device, no servers' is unverifiable pre-release and sits awkwardly next to the option to configure ChatGPT or Grok as providers. No Android. Several unrelated products are also called Halo.

name: shadcn/ui
what: Not a component dependency — a registry you copy Radix-and-Tailwind component source out of, into your own repo, where you then own and edit it. Ships blocks, charts, a theming layer and a CLI that writes the files.
priceDetail: Free. MIT-licensed, no accounts, no paid tier.
notes: The default answer for a React UI layer on client work: because the code lands in the repo rather than in node_modules, there is no upgrade treadmill and no vendor to outlive. It is also what most coding agents already know, so an agent asked for 'a dialog' produces something that matches the rest of the codebase.

Copy-in cuts both ways — you inherit maintenance of every component you pull, and there is no `npm update` to pick up upstream fixes. Worth pinning the registry version you generated from in the project README.
121k GitHub stars showing on the site. Effectively the industry default, which is the real argument for standardising on it rather than on anything more novel.

name: 21st.dev
what: Marketplace of 12,000+ React and Tailwind components, templates and shadcn themes — 2,000+ marketing blocks, 2,100+ UI components — with an MCP endpoint and CLI so an agent can search and install a component without leaving the editor.
priceDetail: The site is browsable without an account. Plan table lists three paid tiers and no free tier: Builder $6/mo, Builder + AI $15/mo (500–2,000 AI credits, top-ups +100 for $5, credits roll over), Team $7.50/seat/mo for 2–50 seats. All figures billed yearly; quarterly is dearer.
notes: The MCP endpoint is the reason to care. Unlimited component retrieval via MCP on any paid tier means an agent building a marketing page pulls real components instead of inventing markup — which is where most agent-built pages fall apart.
Marketplace, not a library: quality varies by contributor, so it wants review before anything reaches a client site. There is no single maintainer standing behind an individual component.

The 21st AI half (multi-model generation, sandbox code mode) is a separate product from the marketplace and priced by credits. Buy the marketplace tier for the components; do not assume the AI credits are worth the difference until someone has tested them.

name: React Bits
what: Collection of animated, interactive React components — text effects, backgrounds, transitions — offered in JS and TS variants with and without Tailwind, copied in by hand or via a CLI.
priceDetail: Free. Licensed MIT + Commons Clause: commercial use of the components in a product is allowed, selling or redistributing the components themselves is not.
notes: Read the licence before shipping. MIT + Commons Clause permits use in client sites and products, but forbids selling, sublicensing or redistributing the components alone, in a bundle, or as a port — so these must not end up inside a Gitwork starter kit or template we hand on or resell.
45,443 stars and a push yesterday, but a single maintainer (David Haz). Fine for copy-in components, where a stalled repo costs us nothing.
Best-in-class for the decorative layer — the text reveals and background effects a landing page needs — which is exactly the work that otherwise eats a day of hand-rolled motion code.

name: Fancy Components
what: Copy-in React components and microinteractions built on Motion and Tailwind — physics-driven text, cursor effects, elastic drags. Deliberately over-the-top rather than a general-purpose UI kit.
priceDetail: Free. MIT licence.
notes: MIT means no restriction on reuse in our own starters, unlike React Bits — worth knowing when picking which library a Gitwork template pulls from.
3,073 stars and last pushed 2026-03-14, so about five months quiet at the time of adding. Copy-in code, so a stalled repo is a low risk; treat anything you copy as ours to maintain.
One person (Daniel Petho). Use it for a specific effect a page needs, not as the foundation of a design system.

name: Motion Primitives
what: Copy-in motion components for React built on Motion and Tailwind — animated lists, dialogs, cursors, text effects — aimed at the layer between a component library and hand-written animation code.
priceDetail: Free. MIT licence.
notes: Assessed from the GitHub repo, not the docs site: motion-primitives.com returned 429 behind a Vercel security checkpoint on every attempt, so nobody here has read the component docs yet. Open it in a browser before relying on it.

The repo states 'This project is in beta. Expect new components to be released regularly and significant updates to the code.' Copy-in code from a beta project means breaking changes are our problem, not an upgrade path.
5,952 stars, MIT, last pushed 2026-03-19 — same five-month quiet spell as Fancy Components, same single-maintainer profile (ibelick).

name: Anime.js
what: General-purpose JavaScript animation engine — timelines, springs, scroll-linked animation, SVG morphing, WAAPI output — driven from one API rather than tied to a framework.
priceDetail: Free. MIT licence (animejs 4.5.0 on npm).
notes: v4 is a full rewrite and is MIT-licensed on npm, which matters because v4 spent time as sponsorware and older write-ups still say it is paid. Check the licence field, not the blog posts.
The reason to reach for it over Motion: it is framework-agnostic, so it covers the Webflow, Framer-embed and plain-HTML work where a React-only motion library is no use.
Effectively one maintainer (Julian Garnier) on a library used everywhere. Low risk — it is a build-time dependency with no service behind it.

name: NumberFlow
what: One component that animates a number changing — digit-by-digit transitions with correct formatting via Intl.NumberFormat, dependency-free, screen-reader friendly. React, Vue and Svelte builds.
priceDetail: Free. MIT licence (@number-flow/react 0.6.2 on npm).
notes: Narrow on purpose, and worth it: animated counters and price toggles appear on nearly every landing page and dashboard we build, and hand-rolled ones almost always break tabular alignment, currency formatting or the accessibility tree. This gets all three right.
Accessible by default — it renders a plain number for assistive tech and animates only the visual layer. That is the part a weekend build gets wrong.
Single maintainer (Maxwell Barvian), 7.6k on GitHub. It is a small MIT dependency with no service attached, so the downside of it going quiet is that we vendor it.

name: Rive
what: Editor plus runtimes for interactive vector animation: build a state machine in the editor, export a .riv file, drive it from code at runtime. Ships runtimes for web, iOS, Android, Flutter, React Native and game engines.
priceDetail: Free $0/seat (3 collaborative files, no .riv export). Cadet $9/seat/mo, 3 seats max, unlimited files and .riv export. Voyager $32/seat/mo, 25 seats max, adds Libraries and embed hosting. Enterprise $120/seat/mo above $10M revenue. Agent credits are extra: $20/seat/mo on Voyager, $40/seat/mo on Enterprise.
notes: The distinction that matters against Lottie: a .riv file carries a state machine, so the animation responds to input at runtime instead of playing a fixed sequence. That is how you ship a genuinely interactive illustration to both web and native from one asset.
Export is behind the paid tier — the free plan cannot produce a .riv — so any client project using Rive needs at least Cadet at $9/seat/mo from day one. Budget it, do not discover it.

Real production credibility (Spotify Wrapped, Duolingo). The cost is that the source of truth lives in Rive's editor rather than in our repo: whoever built the file owns it, and offboarding means re-authoring.

name: Lottielab
what: Browser editor for Lottie animations — import from Figma or SVG, animate, export .lottie/JSON, GIF or MP4, with hosting on a CDN. Aimed at product teams rather than After Effects animators.
priceDetail: Free tier: unlimited files, Lottie and SVG upload, Figma import, GIF and MP4 export. Pro $12 per editor/month billed annually adds Lottie export, HD and 4K video, team library, comments, file-size optimisation and CDN hosting. Enterprise on request.
notes: Lottie export is the paid feature, and Lottie export is the entire point — the free tier is a viewer and a GIF exporter. Treat $12/editor/month as the real price of using it on client work.

The Figma import path is what makes it usable by a designer without After Effects, which is the gap it fills against Rive: simpler tool, dumber output. Lottie plays a fixed sequence and does not react to input.
Their CDN hosting is convenient and a dependency — a client site pulling a .lottie from Lottielab breaks if the account lapses. Self-host the file in the repo instead.

name: Unicorn Studio
what: Layer-based editor for real-time WebGL scenes — 75+ configurable effects, 3D models, extruded text and SVG, pointer and scroll interactivity — published as an embed or exported as JSON for its runtime. Layers rather than a shader node graph.
priceDetail: Free: all 75+ effects, up to 8 publishes with Unicorn branding, personal and non-commercial use only. Legend $168/year or $20/mo: commercial licence, unlimited publishes with no watermark, JSON export, custom 3D models and fonts, versioning, 200 Unicorn AI credits a month.
notes: The free tier is explicitly personal and non-commercial. Any client scene needs Legend at $168/year — using the free plan on paid work is a licence breach, not a grey area.

Redistribution is prohibited on every plan, Legend included: we may use scenes in client deliverables, but we cannot bundle the Unicorn runtime into a Gitwork template or starter kit we hand on. That rules it out of anything productised.

The honest alternative to hand-written shaders for hero sections — a designer can build a gradient or fluid background in an afternoon that would otherwise be a week of GLSL. Watch the performance guide; these ship real GPU cost to mobile.

name: Jitter
what: Browser motion tool aimed at social and product marketing output — import Figma frames, animate on a simple timeline, export 4K video, GIF or Lottie. Templates rather than a blank canvas.
priceDetail: Free tier: unlimited drafts, 3 workspace files, video/GIF/Lottie export capped at 720p 30fps, limited AI credits. Pro is priced per editor/month billed annually and Team above it — both figures render client-side and were not in the served page, so read them in-app before committing.
notes: Fills the gap between 'export a static frame from Figma' and 'open After Effects' for launch and announcement assets — the same surface posts.design covers as reference. 720p/30fps on the free tier means the free plan is for trying it, not shipping.
The Figma import is the whole workflow: it wants the design to exist already, which suits how we work and makes it useless as a design tool in its own right.
Pricing figures unverified — the tier structure is published but the numbers are injected by JavaScript. Do not quote a price to a client from this listing.

name: tldraw
what: Infinite-canvas SDK for React — the whiteboard at tldraw.com is the demo. Multiplayer sync, persistence and shape tooling included; also ships tldraw offline as a local app for you and your agents.
priceDetail: tldraw.com is free to use. The SDK is free in development environments under the tldraw licence; production use needs a commercial licence with a licence key — 100-day free trial, then 'value-based pricing' by arrangement, no public figure.
notes: Read the licence before designing anything around it. The tldraw licence permits development, modification and bundling, but forbids production deployment without a key — a canvas feature demoed to a client on the trial becomes a sales conversation at launch, and the price is not published.

Where it earns its place is scope: multiplayer sync, undo, persistence and hit-testing on an infinite canvas are months of work, and this is the mature option. Used in production by Google, Shopify, Replit and Autodesk per their own site.
49,766 stars, pushed today, real company behind it (tldraw Inc). The free whiteboard is also the fastest way to sketch an architecture diagram with a client on a call — no signup, works on mobile.

name: Paper
what: Design tool built on web standards, pitched at teams shipping with agents — connects the canvas to code and data, and exposes a Paper MCP server so an agent can read and act on the design. Web app plus a desktop build.
priceDetail: Free $0: unlimited viewers and editors, 100 MCP tool calls a week, limited image generation, 25MB image cap. Pro $16 per editor/month billed yearly ($20 monthly): 1M MCP calls a week, 100× image generation, video export, 100MB images. Organisations tier for SSO and custom contracts.
notes: Unusual and worth noting: editors are free, so a whole team can collaborate at $0 — the paywall is on MCP call volume and export, not on seats. That inverts Figma's model and makes it cheap to trial on a real project.
The MCP server is the actual pitch. If an agent can query the design directly, design-to-code stops being an export step. Whether that survives contact with a real build is untested here.
Young product against an entrenched incumbent, and the file format is theirs. Do not put a client's source of truth in it yet; use it where the output is code we own.

name: Penpot
what: Open-source design and prototyping platform, self-hostable, that works in SVG and CSS natively rather than in a proprietary format — so a developer can read the file's actual markup. Plugin API and libraries included.
priceDetail: MPL-2.0 and self-hostable at no licence cost. Hosted plans list $0/user and $7/user/month tiers, with enterprise and support figures on the same page running up to $950/month.
notes: The reason it matters to us is data ownership, not features: self-hosted MPL-2.0 means a client's design files can live inside their own infrastructure, which is an answer we currently do not have for a client who will not put IP in Figma.
58,520 stars, pushed today, a real company and a funded roadmap — this is the credible open-source option, not a hobby project.
It is still behind Figma on polish and on the plugin ecosystem, and self-hosting means we operate it. Only worth proposing when the ownership requirement is real.

name: Mobbin
what: Searchable library of 400,000+ real app and web screenshots — 1,000+ iOS and web apps plus 200 sites — organised by flow (onboarding, paywall, empty state) and by UI element, with recorded animations on paid tiers.
priceDetail: Free tier is capped at the latest 4 apps and 4 sites. Pro $10/month billed yearly (all apps, flows, animations, unlimited collections, screen downloads). Team $16 per member/month billed yearly. Finance+ add-on $399/month for 55+ finance apps.
notes: This is the pattern-research shortcut for client work: instead of arguing about how a paywall or an onboarding flow should behave, pull ten shipped examples in five minutes. $10/month is less than the time it saves on one project.
Free tier is a teaser — 4 apps. Assume Pro if anyone is going to actually use it.
Same IP caution as every reference library here: these are other companies' interfaces. Use them to inform structure and behaviour, never to lift layout or copy into a deliverable.

name: OKLCH Colour Picker & Converter
what: Picker and converter for OKLCH — paste a hex, RGB or HSL value and see it in perceptual colour space, with the sRGB gamut boundary drawn, the closest in-gamut fallback calculated, and a P3 preview. By Evil Martians (Andrey Sitnik and Roman Shamin).
priceDetail: Free, no account.
notes: The practical use is building a palette where every step is perceptually even — lightening a brand colour in HSL shifts its apparent brightness, in OKLCH it does not. That is the fix for the 'why does our hover state look muddy' problem.
It shows the sRGB fallback alongside the P3 value, which is the part people skip: an OKLCH colour outside sRGB renders differently on older displays unless you ship the fallback.
Free tool from a consultancy, no account, nothing to depend on at runtime. Pair it with the APCA contrast guidance they link rather than WCAG 2 ratios.

name: color.review
what: Contrast checker that plots the whole range instead of returning one number — adjust foreground and background and it shows where the pair crosses 3:1, 4.5:1 and 7:1 for text and headlines, with a shareable URL per combination.
priceDetail: Free, no account.
notes: Better than a pass/fail checker for the actual job, which is finding the nearest accessible version of a colour a client has already signed off. The curve shows you how far you have to move, not just that you failed.
URLs encode the pair (color.review/check/293845-FFFFFF), so an accessibility note in a PR or a client email can link to the evidence.
WCAG 2 contrast ratios only. For perceptual accuracy on light text or thin type, cross-check with APCA — the maths behind the 4.5:1 threshold is known to be wrong at the extremes.

name: ray.so
what: Turns a snippet of code into a shareable image — syntax themes, background on or off, dark or light window, padding control. Raycast's own tool, and the source is MIT on GitHub.
priceDetail: Free. MIT licence (raycast/ray-so).
notes: The fastest route from a snippet to something presentable in a deck, a case study or a launch post — the alternative is a screenshot of an editor with someone's file tree in it.
MIT and self-hostable, which matters if we want a Gitwork-themed variant for case studies rather than Raycast's default palettes.
Nothing to depend on: it renders client-side and the output is a PNG or SVG we own.

name: Screen Studio
what: macOS screen recorder that applies automatic zoom on mouse actions and smooths the cursor path, so a raw capture comes out looking edited. Built for product demos and tutorials rather than meetings.
priceDetail: $29/month billed monthly, or $9/month billed yearly. One plan, all features. macOS only — Ventura 13.1+ recommended.
notes: The automatic zoom and cursor smoothing is the entire product, and it is the difference between a demo video a client can put on a landing page and one that looks like a support call. $9/month on annual billing against half a day in an editor per video.
macOS only, so it is a personal-machine tool, not something we can put in a client's hands if they are on Windows.
No free tier listed on the pricing section — plan for the annual figure. Effectively a solo product (Adam Pietrasiak) with a long track record and Product Hunt #1 of the year.

name: Raycast
what: Extensible launcher replacing Spotlight — clipboard history, window management, snippets, script commands and a store of community extensions, with AI and cloud sync on the paid tier. Mac, plus a Windows beta.
priceDetail: Free forever for individuals, including all built-in and community extensions. Pro $10/month monthly or $8/month annual (Raycast AI, unlimited notes, cloud sync, custom themes, translator). Team $15/user/month monthly or $12/user/month annual. Advanced AI add-on +$8/user/month.
notes: The free tier is genuinely the whole launcher — clipboard history and window management alone justify installing it, and nothing is time-limited. Pro buys AI and sync, not the core.
Worth standardising on because extensions are scriptable: a Raycast extension over Foundry's API would put client and task lookup a keystroke away on every machine.
Windows is still beta, so it cannot be the answer for a mixed-OS team yet. The free plan is licensed for organisational use, so there is no compliance reason to avoid it on work machines.

name: Granola
what: Meeting notepad that transcribes locally from the machine's audio rather than joining the call as a bot — you type sparse notes, it merges them with the transcript afterwards. Mac, Windows, mobile and an Apple Watch app.
priceDetail: Basic $0/user/month: AI notes, limited meeting history, AI chat, shared folders, templates. Business $14/user/month: unlimited history, advanced models, integrations (Notion, Slack, HubSpot, Attio, Affinity, Zapier), MCP and API access. Enterprise $35/user/month for SSO and admin controls.
notes: No bot in the call is the point, and it is a client-facing point: nothing announces itself in a prospect meeting, and there is no second participant to consent to. Compare with what Scribe already does inside Foundry before adding another notes silo.
MCP and API access are Business-tier at $14/user/month — that is the tier if we ever want meeting context flowing into Foundry rather than sitting in Granola.

Recording a client call still needs their consent regardless of whether a bot appears; the tool removes the awkwardness, not the obligation. Model-training opt-out is available on every tier, including free.

name: Wispr Flow
what: System-wide voice dictation that rewrites as it goes — punctuation, filler removal and tone applied to speech across any app, in 100+ languages, learning names and jargon from use. Adds a meeting notetaker on Mac.
priceDetail: Free $0/month: dictation across all apps, 100+ languages, Mac/Windows/iOS/Android, notetaker (Mac only), MCP access to notes, HIPAA-ready. Pro $15/user/month monthly or $12/user/month annual: unlimited dictations, longer meeting retention, advanced models. Enterprise on request.
notes: Where it pays off is prompting: dictating a long, specific brief to a coding agent is several times faster than typing it, and the cleanup is what separates this from built-in dictation.
The free tier caps dictation volume rather than features, so the real cost of adopting it across the team is $12/user/month on annual billing.

$81M raised and enterprise compliance claims (SOC 2 Type II, ISO 27001) — but everything dictated passes through their processing. Model-training opt-out exists on every tier; check it before dictating anything under a client NDA.

name: LocalSend
what: Cross-platform file transfer over the local network with no cloud, no account and no internet — Windows, macOS, Linux, Android and iOS, using an encrypted peer-to-peer connection between devices on the same Wi-Fi.
priceDetail: Free and open source. No ads or trackers per the project's own claim.
notes: The practical case is AirDrop across an OS boundary: getting a build, a video or a set of assets from a Mac to an Android test device or a Windows machine without uploading a client's files to a third party.
Because it never leaves the local network, it is the safe answer for moving anything covered by an NDA between machines — no service to audit, no retention policy to read.
70k+ stars and 5M+ downloads claimed on the site. Open source with contributors rather than a company; a stalled release cycle costs nothing since the protocol is local.

name: Radix UI
what: The unstyled, accessible primitives shadcn/ui is built on — dialog, popover, select, dropdown and the rest, each handling focus trapping, keyboard interaction and ARIA, with no styling opinions. Also ships Themes, an Icons set and the Colors scales.
priceDetail: Free and open source, MIT. Maintained by WorkOS.
notes: Worth listing separately from shadcn/ui because it is the layer underneath: when a copied shadcn component behaves oddly on keyboard or screen reader, the answer is in Radix's docs, not shadcn's.
The accessibility work is the product. Focus management on a nested dialog, or type-ahead on a select, is a fortnight of subtle bugs to reimplement and the reason not to hand-roll these.
Backed by a funded company rather than a lone maintainer, which is unusual in this list and matters for anything a client depends on for years.

name: Sonner
what: One toast component for React, by Emil Kowalski — `npm install sonner`, render `<Toaster />` at the root, call `toast()` anywhere. Stacking, swipe-to-dismiss and promise states are handled.
priceDetail: Free, MIT.
notes: It is the toast shadcn/ui itself now recommends, so standardising on it means an agent-written component and a hand-written one agree on how notifications work.
Narrow and finished — the promise API (`toast.promise`) covers the loading/success/error pattern that otherwise gets rebuilt badly on every project.
One maintainer, but it is a small MIT dependency with no service behind it, so the downside is vendoring it.

name: dnd kit
what: Drag-and-drop toolkit written in TypeScript — framework-agnostic core with first-class React, Vue, Svelte and Solid packages, plus sortable lists, custom sensors, modifiers and a plugin layer.
priceDetail: Free and open source.
notes: Drag-and-drop is the classic underestimate: pointer, touch and keyboard sensors, collision detection, auto-scroll and accessible announcements are months of work, and clients ask for reorderable lists constantly.
Keyboard sensors mean a sortable list is operable without a mouse, which is the difference between a feature and an accessibility complaint.
The rewrite splits into a framework-agnostic core with per-framework bindings, so a Vue or Svelte client project is no longer a reason to pick a different library.

name: SVGL
what: Library of brand logos as clean SVGs, categorised (AI 67, Adobe 56, Design 62, Database 23 and so on), with light and dark variants, a public API, a shadcn/ui registry entry and editor extensions.
priceDetail: Free, open source, no account.
notes: Solves a job we do on nearly every client site — the logo wall, the integrations grid, the tech-stack strip — where the alternative is hunting press kits and tracing PNGs.
The API and the shadcn registry mean an agent building a logo section can fetch the real mark instead of inventing one.

Third-party trade marks. Fine for showing genuine integrations or clients; get permission before implying an endorsement, and check each brand's own guidelines for a logo you are putting in front of the public.

name: Phosphor Icons
what: Icon family in six weights — thin through to fill, plus duotone — designed as one system so a whole interface can shift weight without redrawing anything. By Helena Zhang and Tobias Fried, with React, Vue, Svelte, Flutter and web-component packages.
priceDetail: Free, MIT.
notes: The six-weight system is the reason to choose it over Lucide or Heroicons: a dense dashboard and a marketing page can share an icon set and still look right, because weight carries the difference.
MIT, so unlike most icon sets there is nothing to check before it ships in a client deliverable or a Gitwork starter.

The browsing site needs JavaScript and served nothing readable without it, so the family was assessed from its own description and packages rather than by browsing the set. Open it in a browser to pick icons.

name: Iconbuddy
what: Search across 300,000+ icons from open-source sets in one place — Phosphor, Tabler, Material, Solar, Lucide and dozens more — recolour and resize in the browser, then export SVG, PNG, JSX or Base64. Figma, VS Code, Framer and Chrome plugins.
priceDetail: Free search and download. Pro $6.99/month, $49.99/year, or $120 once for lifetime. Team from 3 seats × $39/year = $117/year.
notes: The value is the search across sets: finding the one icon that matches a client's existing set without installing five libraries to compare.

The icons themselves come from their original open-source projects and keep those licences — Iconbuddy sells the search and the export, not the artwork, so check the source set's licence for anything unusual.
$120 lifetime is the sane option if anyone here uses it weekly; the monthly is hard to justify against free browsing on the source sites.

name: Thiings
what: Collection of 10,000+ AI-generated 3D icons in a single consistent style — objects, tools, food, tech — downloadable individually or as the whole set with JSON metadata.
priceDetail: Personal $0: individual downloads, non-commercial only, attribution required. Indie $49 lifetime for businesses under $200k/year revenue. Business $199 lifetime for over $200k. Enterprise above $2M/year or 50+ staff. Reselling the icons as assets is excluded on every tier.
notes: Read the licence before it touches client work. The free tier is non-commercial with attribution, and their own terms say that when you are buying on behalf of a client you pick the tier matching the client's revenue, not ours — so a big client's site needs the $199 tier even though we bought it.
One consistent 3D style across 10,000 objects is genuinely hard to source; the usual alternative is commissioning renders or accepting a mismatched stock set.
AI-generated artwork, so treat provenance as unsettled for anything a client will trade mark or put on packaging.

name: unDraw
what: Open-source SVG illustration collection by Katerina Limpitsouni — pick a hex colour on the site and every illustration recolours to it before download.
priceDetail: Free, open licence, no attribution required.
notes: No attribution required is the differentiator against most free illustration sets, and it is what makes it usable on a client deliverable without a credits line.
The on-site recolour means a set can be pulled straight into a client's brand colour instead of arriving in someone else's purple.
So widely used that it reads as a placeholder to anyone in the industry. Fine for internal tools, empty states and prototypes; a poor choice for a brand-led marketing page.

name: Storyset
what: Customisable illustrations with an online editor — change colours, swap components and animate a scene, then export as static SVG or an animated asset. Themed sets for business, education, medical, technology and people, plus a Figma plugin.
priceDetail: Free to use and download. Run by Freepik; attribution terms were not readable in the served page, so check the licence on the asset before it ships.
notes: The animation export is the part unDraw does not do — an animated empty state or onboarding step without opening After Effects.

Freepik's free assets normally require attribution unless you hold a subscription, and the licence page did not render for us. Confirm before putting one on a client site, because retro-fitting a credit line is awkward.
Same house-style problem as unDraw, more so. Rated Low deliberately: useful for speed on internal or throwaway work, not for anything brand-led.

name: CleanShot X
what: Screenshot and screen-recording app for Mac with the parts the built-in tool lacks — scrolling capture, annotation, self-timer, hidden desktop icons, OCR, and an upload that returns a shareable link.
priceDetail: $29 one-time for the Mac app and 1GB cloud, keep it forever; updates optional at $19/year after the first year. App + Cloud Pro $8 per user/month billed annually, or $10/month monthly. 30-day money-back guarantee.
notes: The one-time $29 licence with optional renewal is unusually honest pricing, and it makes this the cheap default for every machine here — the app keeps working if you never renew.
Scrolling capture and annotation are the day-to-day wins: a full-page screenshot of a client site with callouts, in one pass, instead of stitching three images.
Different job from Screen Studio, which is for polished demo video. This is for the twenty captures a day that go into Slack, tickets and QA notes.

name: Shottr
what: Small, fast Mac screenshot app aimed at people who care about pixels — scrolling screenshots, OCR, annotation, and measurement tools for checking spacing and colour against a design. A 2.3MB download.
priceDetail: Free to download and use; the site sells a licence via its Buy page, but no figure was present in the served pricing text.
notes: The measurement instruments are the reason it is here rather than CleanShot: measuring spacing straight off the screen is exactly the front-end QA loop when a build is drifting from the design.
2.3MB and native, so it is a reasonable thing to put on every machine even alongside CleanShot X.
Pricing unverified — free is what the download page offers, and the licence figure was not readable, so do not quote a cost from this listing.

name: Xnapper
what: Mac screenshot app that beautifies automatically — balanced padding, background, rounded corners and, notably, automatic redaction of detected emails and sensitive text before you share.
priceDetail: One-time: Basic $29.99 (1 Mac), Personal $54.99 (2 Macs), Standard $79.99 (3 Macs), each with a year of updates and optional renewal at 40% off. Team $5 per device/month billed annually.
notes: Automatic redaction is the feature worth paying for on client work — screenshots of a staging environment routinely leak real customer emails into a Slack channel or a deck.
Overlaps heavily with CleanShot X at more than twice the price. Pick one; this wins only if the auto-redaction and instant beautifying matter more than scrolling capture and cloud links.
Per-device licensing means a laptop and a studio Mac need the $54.99 tier, not the $29.99.

name: Cap
what: Open-source Loom alternative for macOS, Windows and Linux. Instant Mode gives a shareable link in seconds; Studio Mode is a local editor with zoom and layout controls. Self-hostable, so recordings can stay on infrastructure you own.
priceDetail: Free forever for personal use, unlimited local recordings. Desktop Licence $29/year, perpetual. Cap Pro $8.16 per user/month for the hosted side. Open source on GitHub and self-hostable.
notes: Self-hosting is the argument. A walkthrough of a client's admin panel recorded to Loom's servers is their data on a third party's infrastructure; the same recording on our own instance is not a conversation with their security team.
Cross-platform, unlike Screen Studio and CleanShot, so it is the one screen-recording answer we can give a client on Windows.
Free tier is genuinely usable for local recordings — the paid tiers buy hosted sharing and team features, not the recorder.

name: Arcade
what: Interactive product demos: capture a flow in the browser extension or desktop app and it becomes a clickable walkthrough rather than a video, with branching, CTAs, personalisation and an MCP endpoint. Also generates AI voiceovers and videos from the same capture.
priceDetail: Free $0/month: unlimited AI demos, 1 published demo, 1 published video, 200 AI credits a month. Growth $42.50 per seat/month billed yearly ($50 monthly): branding, translations, branching, CTAs and insights. Enterprise on request.
notes: The pitch that matters for us is client-facing: an interactive demo of a build we shipped is a better case-study artefact than a video, because the reader drives it and it survives on a phone.
The free tier's one published demo makes it a trial, not a plan — real use starts at $42.50 a seat.
Demos are hosted by Arcade and embedded, so a case study built on it dies if the account lapses. Keep a video capture of anything that matters.

name: Rotato
what: 3D mockup generator for Mac — drop a screenshot or a live URL onto a device model, then rotate, light and animate it from any angle and export 4K stills or video. 30+ devices and 80+ ready-made templates.
priceDetail: Free to download and use on any Mac. Paid plans are listed at $239/year and $861/year; the pricing page frames these against hiring a 3D artist rather than itemising what each tier includes, so confirm in-app before buying.
notes: Fills the app-store-screenshot and case-study-hero job: an animated device mockup of a client build, without opening Blender or buying a template pack that dates in a year.
The device library is the perishable part — a mockup on last year's iPhone reads as stale, and staying current is exactly what the subscription buys.
Pricing is the least clear of anything in this batch. The free tier is real and worth trying first; get the tier details in writing before it goes on a client budget.

name: FontBase
what: Font manager for Mac, Windows and Linux — activate and deactivate families without installing them system-wide, organise by collection, preview with your own text, and pull in Google Fonts directly.
priceDetail: Core font management is free on all three platforms. The Awesome tier adds features from around $3/month.
notes: The practical case is per-project activation: a Mac with 400 client fonts installed slows every design app and pollutes every font menu. Activating only the families for the project in hand fixes that.
Cross-platform, which matters if anyone here works on Windows — most font managers are Mac-only.
It manages fonts, it does not license them. Keeping a client's licensed families organised does not make them ours to reuse on the next project.

name: Realtime Colors
what: Applies a palette and type pairing to a full dummy website in the browser and updates live as you change them — so a colour scheme is judged on a real page with real hierarchy instead of as swatches. Figma plugin and a VS Code theme editor.
priceDetail: Free, no account.
notes: It answers the question swatches cannot: what a palette does to a whole page. Most palettes that die in review died because nobody saw them at page scale until it was built.
Sharing a URL of a live palette is a faster client conversation than a PDF of colour chips, and it removes the 'it looked different in the deck' argument.
Judgement aid, not an accessibility check. Run the pairs through color.review or an APCA tool before committing — a palette can look right here and still fail contrast.

name: Conductor
what: Runs several coding agents at once, each in its own isolated workspace, so parallel work does not collide in one checkout. Local workspaces on a Mac on the free tier; Conductor Cloud runs them in cloud sandboxes.
priceDetail: Free $0: parallel agents in local workspaces on your Mac, bring your own model subscriptions and keys. Pro $50/month adds Conductor Cloud workspace hours, multiplayer, the API and teams up to 5. Teams $60/month per user above that.
notes: Directly relevant to how we already work: the constraint on running three Claude Code sessions is that they fight over one working tree, and isolated workspaces per agent is precisely that fix.
The free tier is local-only but complete for one machine, and you bring your own Claude subscription — so there is no second model bill to trial it.

Cloud sandboxes mean client code leaving our machines. Check what a client's contract says about third-party processing before pointing Conductor Cloud at their repo; the local tier avoids the question entirely.

name: OpenCode
what: Open-source terminal coding agent with a desktop build for macOS, Windows and Linux. Model-agnostic — ships with free models included and connects to Claude, GPT, Gemini or any provider you hold a key for.
priceDetail: Free and open source. Model costs are whatever provider you point it at; some models are included at no cost.
notes: The reason to know it: it is the credible open-source answer to Claude Code, and being model-agnostic it is the fallback if a client forbids a specific vendor or we need a local model on sensitive work.
Being open source, its prompts and tool definitions are readable — genuinely useful reference when writing our own agent tooling in Foundry.
Not a reason to move off Claude Code for day-to-day work. List it as the second option, and try it on an internal project before it touches a client repo.

name: CodeRabbit
what: AI pull-request reviewer that comments line by line with context from the whole repo, offers one-click fixes, runs linters and SAST tools, and learns from how a team responds to its past reviews. Integrates with Jira and Linear.
priceDetail: Pro $24/month per user billed annually. Pro Plus $48/month per user adds multi-repo analysis and custom pre-merge checks. CodeRabbit Security $40/month per user. Slack agent billed at $0.50 per agent minute. 14-day free trial, no card.
notes: The case for a studio is consistency: every PR gets the same review even when the person who would have caught it is on another project. It does not replace review, it stops the obvious things reaching a human.
$24 a seat is real money against Claude Code already reviewing diffs on request. Trial it on one repo and measure whether it catches things we did not before committing the team.
It reads every client repo you connect it to. That is a processor relationship needing checking against client contracts, and the reason the Security tier exists separately.

name: Firecrawl
what: Turns any URL or whole site into clean Markdown or structured JSON for an agent to consume — handles JavaScript rendering, crawling and extraction behind one API, with a search endpoint on top.
priceDetail: Free 1,000 credits/month, 2 concurrent requests. Hobby $16/month (5,000 pages). Standard $83/month (100,000 pages, 50 concurrent). Growth $333/month (500,000). Scale $599/month (1,000,000). All billed yearly; extra credits sold on top. Open source.
notes: This is the thing we keep hand-rolling. Every audit and content migration starts with 'fetch these pages and give me the text', and the fiddly parts — JS rendering, rate limits, boilerplate stripping — are exactly what this sells.
Open source with a hosted tier, so a sensitive client crawl can run on our own infrastructure while everyday work uses the hosted API.
Free tier is 1,000 pages a month, which genuinely covers a small site audit. Watch the credit model on a large crawl — a 100k-page site is the $83 tier, not the $16.

name: Exa
what: Search API built for agents rather than people — semantic search over the live web returning full page contents, plus crawling and a deep-research endpoint, priced per request instead of per seat.
priceDetail: Free tier to start, then usage-based — search priced per thousand results and contents per page, with published unit rates from around $0.01 per request. No seat licence.
notes: Relevant to Foundry rather than to client sites: an agent that needs current information — competitor pages, a client's own live site, a standard that changed — needs a search API, and general web search results are shaped for humans.
Usage pricing means a runaway agent loop is a bill, not a rate-limit error. Cap it before wiring it into anything automated.
Verified the pricing model but not the per-tier detail; the published rates are unit prices, so model expected volume before committing.

name: Composio
what: Gives an agent authenticated tool access to 1,000+ apps — Gmail, Slack, Notion, GitHub and the rest — handling OAuth on behalf of a user, sandboxed execution and parallel tool calls, so you do not build an integration per service.
priceDetail: Free $0/month to start, then $29/month and $229/month tiers with per-execution rates around $0.25–$0.30 above the included volume.
notes: The hard part it sells is delegated auth: holding a user's Google or Slack credentials safely so an agent can act as them. That is the part we should not be building ourselves for Foundry.
It becomes a custodian of client and staff credentials for every app you connect. That is a security review before adoption, not after — and a reason to scope it to internal tools first.

Worth flagging: their homepage carries text addressed to AI agents reading the HTML, pointing at their signup flow. Harmless here, but it is a live example of why an agent browsing the web needs to treat page content as untrusted input rather than instructions.

name: Steel
what: Open-source browser infrastructure for agents — managed headless Chrome sessions over an API, with session reuse, proxies and captcha handling, driven from Puppeteer, Playwright or Selenium.
priceDetail: Free $0 tier, then plans at $30, $100 and $250/month. Open source and self-hostable.
notes: Where Firecrawl reads pages, this drives them — the option when a job needs a logged-in session or a form filled, which is most real client migrations.
Open source and self-hostable, so a client's credentials need not sit in a third party's browser session.
Same note as Composio: the site embeds a line addressed to AI agents pointing at its setup instructions. Read it as marketing aimed at crawlers, not as guidance to follow.

name: TinyPNG
what: Image compression in the browser for WebP, AVIF, JXL, PNG and JPEG, with format conversion, a website analyser that estimates the savings available on any URL, and a developer API for automating it in a build.
priceDetail: Free in the browser for everyday batches. The developer API is metered, with a free monthly allowance before paid usage.
notes: Still the fastest fix for the most common client complaint we get about performance — a 4MB hero image someone exported from Figma at full size.
The site analyser is the useful half for us: point it at a client's live URL and get a number for the savings, which is a better argument in a report than 'optimise your images'.
Next.js and Vercel already optimise images at build and request time, so this is for assets outside that pipeline — email, decks, uploads to a CMS — rather than for the app itself.

name: Dropover
what: Mac drag-and-drop shelf: shake the pointer mid-drag and a floating tray appears to hold files, links, text or images, so you can gather from several places and drop them all at once instead of one window at a time.
priceDetail: Free to download and use.
notes: Small but constant: collecting assets from four folders into a client upload, or pulling files out of a download folder into a project, is a daily task and macOS makes it needlessly fiddly.
Native and unobtrusive — it appears only when you shake mid-drag, so it costs nothing when unused.
Handles files, links, text and images in one shelf, which makes it a staging area for a deck or a handover rather than only a file mover.
